239. These are, in a nutshell, depositions of the witnesses in this case, we find that those witnesses maybe categorised in three categories of which the (a) 1st group of witnesses deposed in the case coming from Central Jail, Dhaka (b )while the 2nd group of witnesses coming from Bangabhaban yet the (c) third group of witnesses are those who do not belong to the said two groups whose testimonies are also material for the purpose of this case; out of the first group of witnesses who are coming from the Central Jail they are PW I Deputy Inspector General of Prisons and the informant in the case, PW 2 the Jailor, PW 3 Inspector General of Prisons, PW 4 a Jail Guard, PW 5 Gate Security of the Central Jail, PW 6 another Jail Guard, PW 7 Deputy Jailor, PW 8 another Deputy Jailor, PW 9 Chief Jail Guard, PW 12 another Jail Guard PW 20 Mahbubuddin Ahmed, former Superintendent of Police and a detenu of the Central Jail; at the relevant time and PW 22 Dr Rafique Uddin Ahmed, Assistant Surgeon, serving in Central Jail while the 2nd group coming from Bangabhaban they are PW 11, Assistant PS to Military Secretary to the President, PW 13 a khedmathker, PW 16 a telephone operator engaged in Bangabhaban PW 17 a receptionist/PA of Bangabhaban PW 18 another khedrnathker, PW 21 Commodore Golam Rabbani, ADC to the President, PW 34 receptionist of Bangabhaban. The third group of witnesses are the remaining witnesses in the case out of whom the testimonies of PW 29, PW 46 and 52 are of vital importance in the decision of this case and that PWs 29 Colonel Shafayet Jamil, second man in the coup headed by Khaled Mosharaf and PW 46A Major at the relevant time PW 52 Syed Mahbub-al- Karim, a Special Officer of slain leader Syed Nazrul Islam while the remaining witnesses of this category may be termed as formal witnesses in this case.

240. From the depositions of those witnesses we find that the prosecution led evidence to bring home before the Court, two aspects of the case such as, 5 defence personnel had entered into the Central Jail, Dhaka at the dawn of 3-11-75 at the behest of army officers residing at Bangabhaban at the relevant time and those 5 persons had perpetrated the crime by opening brush fire upon the 4 leaders of Awami League namely, Syed Nazrul Islam, Tajuddin Ahmed, Captain Monsur Ali and Mr Karnruzzaman. The witnesses coming from the Jail had also made an attempt to connect the officers residing at the Bangabhaban by way of telephonic conversation in between the Bangabhaban and Central Jail at the relevant time. The other part of the case as the prosecution wanted to make out is that the Army officers then residing at Bangabhaban at the relevant time had been in close link with the President and in collusion with each other had conspired and abetted the crime perpetrated by those 5 defence personnel who had entered inside the Central Jail and for those purposes the witnesses deposed before the Court disclosing about the telephonic conversations between Bangabhaban and Central Jail by some of those officers residing in Bangabhaban. It has also been attempted to show that at about midnight some officers including Captain Moslemuddin had left Bangabhaban being armed, with an army jeep and at the next dawn they had returned back to Bangabhaban so the factum of going out and getting in to Bangabhaban was attempted to be proved by the prosecution showing certain circumstances coupled with telephonic conversation to prove the complicity of the accused persons by way of abetment in the crime.

241. From a perusal of the impugned judgment we have already noticed that the charge was framed in the case on 3 counts of which the first one was under section 120B against all the 20 accused persons (since one of them died before framing of the charge) while the other one was framed against 19 accused persons except Captain Muslemuddin under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code while a separate charge under section 302 of the Penal Code was framed against Captain/Resalder Muslemuddin alias Muslemuddin alias Hiron Khan.

242. We have further noticed that the charge under section 120B of the Penal Code had failed before the trial Court, therefore, the learned Metropolitan Sessions Judge has acquitted all the accused persons from the charge under section 120B of the Penal Code and the said order of acquittal has not been challenged. We have further noticed that of the 20 accused persons charged under sections 302/] 09, 5 of them have also been acquitted from the charge under sections 302/109 of the Penal Code and they are (1) Major Khairuzzaman (2) Taher Uddin Thakur (3) KM Obaidur Rahman and (4) Nurul Islam Monjur.

243. The aforesaid order of acquittal has not also been challenged by anyone at any stage.

244. We have noticed further that out of said 20, 15 accused persons (except 5 acquitted persons) have been convicted under sections 302/109 of the Penal Code sentencing each of them thereunder to imprisonment for life with fine of Tk.10,000 each, in default, to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 6(six) months.

245. On the third count out of the aforesaid 15 persons convicted under sections 302/109 of the Penal Code, 3 have also been convicted under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code sentencing each of them thereunder to capital punishment along with fine of Tk.10,000 each, they are (I) Resalder MosIcmuddin alias Moslemuddin (Retd) alias Hiron Khan alias Muslemuddin (2) Dafader Marfat Ali Shah and (3) LD (Dafader) Md Abul Hashem Mridha, therefore, it appears that the aforesaid three accused persons who have been condemned to death have also been sentenced to imprisonment for life under sections 302/109 of the Penal Code.

246. It may not be out of context to mention that the death sentence of the aforesaid 3 accused persons have been sent before this Court in the instant Death Reference No.150 of 2004 along with the other appellants before us who have preferred separate Criminal Appeals, they are Lieutenant Colonel Farook Rahman, Lieutenant Colonel Sultan Shahriar Rashid Khan, Major (Retd) Bazlul Huda and Major (Retd) AKM Mohiuddin Ahmed, therefore, it is evident that we are required to review the case of 3 condemned prisoners namely, Resalder Moslemuddin alias Moslemuddin (Retd) alias Hiron Khan alias Moslemuddin, Dafader Marfat Ali Shah and Ld (Dafader) Md Abul Hashem Mridha along with the 4 appellants named above.

247. In this case we have already seen that there are discrepancies available in respect of the first information report since we have already noticed that the prosecution has made an attempt to prove Exhibits 1 and 3 as the first information report in the instant case and such attempt has been made through PW I who deposed in connection with Exhibit 1 to the effect that it is a copy of the first information report not the original one and the same had been collected from the Jail but in this connection this witness, during his cross-examination denied the specific suggestion given to him to the effect that the ejahar that has been collected through him, had been forged by PW 1. This witness also admitted in his cross-examination that Exhibit 1 did not contain any Memo number, he has however asserted that at the bottom of this paper a memo number was available which was Memo No. 11 DIG/ 11(4) dated Dacca 4-11-75 and it was the memo number of his office. This witness also admitted further that the copy of the first information report that had been seized from him did not contain the same number. This witness admitted further that the Exhibit 3 did not contain any memo number, in this connection we have ourselves gone though the said Exhibit 1 as available from the Lower Courts record wherefrom it transpires that in the memo number as quoted by PW 1 in Exhibit I there are over writings such sort of over writing is also available in the date of the said memo. It is also visible through bare eyes that Exhibit 1 contains a signature purported to be of the informant but the said signature contain a date which is 4-11-76 which date has no relevance whatsoever with this case. This is the position of the first information report as disclosed above, produced by PW 1 and had been marked as Exhibit 1. In this connection PW 64 the Investigating Officer has also admitted in his cross-examination that after taking over the charge of investigation he did not find any judicial record even he did not get the first information report, he had simply got the GR number. In respect of Exhibit 3 the other piece of paper which has been claimed by the prosecution as an first information report, This PW 64 deposed in his cross-examination that he had got a copy of the first information report marked as Exhibit 3 from the Office of the Inspector General of Police but it was not seized by any seizure list nor did he seize the record from which he had collected this piece of paper. It is also admitted by PW 64 that he had not investigated as to with what reference Exhibit 3 had gone to the office of the Inspector General of Police. In this connection PW 1 has admitted in his cross- examination that the copy of the first information report which has been marked as Exhibit did not contain his (informant) signature.

248. With respect to the first information report PW 1 in his cross-examination admitted further that he had lodged the first information report after consultation with the Inspector General of Prisons and other officials of the Central Jail.

249. In the backdrop as aforesaid, with respect to the first information report in this case Mr ASM Mobin, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the State has submitted that in a case where there is no first information report or in a case where the first information report could not be proved in accordance with law in that case too it would not detract the contents of the testimonies of the direct witnesses available in the case and in substantiating his submission Mr Mobin has referred to the case of Rehman vs State, reported in PLD 1968 Lahore 464 (relevant page 470 para-13), Mr Mobin also referred to the decision in the case of Somappa Vamanappa Madar Shankarappa Ravanappa Kaddi vs State of Mysore reported in AIR 1979 (SC) 1831 (1836) para 12. From a perusal of the aforesaid judgment we find Exhibit P-9 was treated as an first information report in that case, the defence took objection that the said first information report was recorded after initiation of the investigation in the case because it could be detected by the Court also that the said Exhibit P-9 was recorded in course of investigation of the case, therefore, it was rightly objected to by the defence and under such circumstances the Supreme Court of India held that the rejection of Exhibit P-9 as first information report would not detract the testimony of the eye-witnesses which would have to be assessed on its own merits. Therefore, even in view of such defect of Exhibit P- 9 the Supreme Court of India had entered into the evidence and assessed the same then concluded the case on merit.

250. The learned Assistant Attorney-General also placed reliance in the case of Rehman vs State reported in PLD 1968 Lahore 464 wherefrom it transpires that a similar situation had arisen in that case in respect of the first information report where- upon, a Division Bench of Lahore High Court although held that it was true that the absence of the first information report deprives the accused of his right to cross-examine the first informant on its basis. However, the fact that no first information report was made or was proved at the trial could not vitiate the conviction. But in the concluding part of the judgment it was observed as follows:

"In this case also, the first information regarding the murder of Mst Haleeman (deceased) was that entered in Exhibit PA which was neither produced nor proved, instead Exhibit PW 15/ A a copy of the first information report No. 169 of 1965, was produced at the trial. Since the first information report in question itself was recorded on the basis of Exhibit P A and contained neither the signatures nor thumb impression of Mutalli PW 8 (the informant) its copy Exhibit PW 15/ A cannot properly fall within the definition of "first information" and, therefore, it should have been excluded from consideration by the trial Court. However, it is to be noted that the absence of first information report deprives the accused of his right to cross- examine the informant on its basis which as a result is bound to prejudice his case in some measure, It is, therefore, the duty of the prosecution to prove the first information report where it exists, so that the accused is not subjected to any handicap in the defence of his case. Be that as it may, since Exhibit PW 15/ A cannot be taken into consideration the prosecution case must now depend on the evidence of eye-witnesses."

251. In view of the aforesaid two decisions cited by the learned Assistant Attorney-General we find neither Exhibit 1 nor Exhibit 3 can be treated as first information report in this case though these two papers, as it could be gathered from attending circumstances, undoubtedly contain the contents of the report made by PW 1 first in point of time with Lalbagh Police Station on 4-11-1975.

252. In view of the deposition of PW 1 and PW 64 as referred to above, we are of the considered opinion that the two documents cannot be treated as an first information report in the instant case since neither of the two falls within the purview of the definition of an first information report as contemplated under section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. But at the same time relying on the two decisions we are of the view that the prosecution case, in the instant case, depends on testimonies of the witnesses available in this case, therefore, let us proceed with the evaluation of the evidence already on record.

253. Before we proceed with the assessment of evidence of PW 1, DIG (Prisons) we may take into consideration the contents of the Exhibit 1 which PW 1 himself claims to be the report what he had made, first in point of time with Lalbagh Police Station on 4-11-75. From a plain reading of Exhibit 1 we find PW 1 made a report to the effect that on 3- 11-75 at about 4-00 AM one army officer wearing khaki dress disclosing his identity of being attached to Bangabhaban, accompanied by 4 other army personnel wearing khaki dress came to the Jail Gate with Stengun, SLR etc. Entered into the Jail Gate and killed the 4 leaders (1) Syed Nazrul Islam (2) Tajuddin Ahmed (3) Captain Monsur Ali (4) AHM Kamruzzaman further details about the incident would be furnished in due course. The dead bodies of 4 persons were still lying in Jail and he prayed for necessary action in this regard. That was the report he made one day after the occurrence before the police. But long thereafter in the year 1996 this witness was examined by the Investigating Officer with an inordinate delay, the prosecution has however explained the same assigning the reasons and in course of examination of this witness by the Investigating Officer he had narrated a story similar to the one disclosed by him before the trial Court but during cross-examination his attention was drawn to the report he had made earlier before the police and the Magistrate before whom he had made a statement which was recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In his cross- examination this witness admitted that he had made the report in a condensed form and indeed he has made many a disclosure before the trial Court beyond his said report dated 4-11-1975 i. e Exhibit 1. This witness also admitted in his cross-examination that it was at his asking the assailants had gone to the Jail Gate and put their signatures in the gate register. During his cross-examination this witness however admitted that he could not say whether the accused persons used to reside at Bangabhaban before the occurrence. He does not know the telephone number of any of the accused and with none of the accused he had any talk prior to the occurrence. He also admitted that he did not have any telephonic conversation with the accused per- sons. This witness also admitted in his cross- examination that Major Rashid whom he referred in his deposition was not known to him from before and he had not seen him earlier. He also admitted that unless the man is known to him from before one cannot identify some one by his voice over telephone. This witness also denied his knowledge as to whether the gate register where the assailants put their signatures before they had entered into the Jail were produced before the Court or not. This witness also admitted in his cross-examination that while he was working in Sylhet there was a proceeding against him in connection with a bail bond and in that proceeding he was exonerated as he tendered his unconditional apology. This witness also admitted in his cross-examination that he did not know that on the night following November, 2 1975 was there any correspondence between Bangabhaban and the Central Jail, Dhaka. With respect to Exhibit 2 this witness deposed that it does not contain his signature. He also deposed that a copy of Exhibit 2 which he retained with him was a carbon copy of the original and in the body of Exhibit 2 he had written a date as 05-11-75 which is a typed date, but he also admitted at the same time that the original report contains a hand written date 5-11-75 He also denied his knowledge as to whether Exhibit 2 is similar to the one retained by him.

254. In view of the aforesaid position in the deposition of PW 1 and in view of his admission to the effect that he had disclosed many a thing before the Court which were not there in the purported first information report, we are not in a position to place reliance in the evidence of PW 1. In this connection more particularly when the Exhibit 1 does not contain name of the accused persons except Captain Moslemuddin. Similar view has also been taken by the trial Court in the impugned judgment with respect to PW 1 with which we find no reason to differ.

255. PW 2 Md Aminur Rahman, Jailor at the relevant time, in his examination in chief, had disclosed that at about 4-00 AM on the fateful night he had received 5 Army personal at the Jail Gate all of them put their signatures in the gate register, thereafter he took those 5 persons to the office of the Deputy Inspector General of Prisons but the gate register which contained the signatures of the 5 assailants was never produced before the Court. This witness also deposed that Captain Moslem and 4 other persons were armed and they had uniforms with khaki as also of black colour and they had no badge on their shoulder. This witness also deposed that the 4 persons who had entered into the Central Jail subsequent to the first occurrence had also put their signatures in the gate register. This witness also admitted in his deposition that he had instructed the guards to resist those if anyone had attempted to enter inside the Jail but it appears from his examination in chief that he had himself received those 5 persons and took them to the office of the DIG (prisons), this witness denied the suggestion that he had not made any statement before the Investigating Officer to the effect that Major Rashid had a conversation with him over telephone. This witness also admitted in his cross-examination to the effect that there is a provision in the Jail Code that none without any written order can enter inside the Jail but we find this witness has admitted that he himself received the 5 assailants at the Jail Gate. This witness admitted that the barracks of the sepoys situate at the opposite side of the Jail Gate and on the night of occurrence BDR personnel were kept alert with arms, This witness also admitted in his cross- examination to the effect “ ঘটনার রাত্রে কারাগারে পাগলা ঘন্টি বাজানো হয়।”

256. This witness further admitted that when alarm was raised in that case, order for use of arms could be passed. He also admitted that under the provision of Jail Code the Jail guard can use the arms to save the lives of the inmates of the Jail. This witness also admitted in his cross-examination to the effect that :

“ বহিরাগত দুষ্কৃতিকারী জেলের অভ্যন্তরে প্রবেশ করিয়া জোরপূর্বক কিছু সংখ্যক আসামীকে ছিনিয়া নিতে পারে এই মর্মে ঘটনার রাত্রিতে আইজি(প্রিজন) আমাকে জানায় এবং সতর্ক থাকার জন্য বলেন, ইহা সত্য।”

257. We have also noted the depositions of this witness in the first part of the judgment and in view of the position as aforesaid we do not find that this witness is a trustworthy one because his disclosure amounts to travesty of truth. In this connection we are also of the opinion that we have no reason to dis- agree with the findings of the trial Court in respect of this witness (PW 2), we find that he has discarded the testimonies of this witness with cogent reasons.

258. PW 3 ATM Nuruzzaman, Inspector General of Prisons, whose depositions we have already noted in the earlier part of this judgment; his evidence has also thoroughly been discussed and evaluated by the trial Court. The deposition of PW 3 shows that he had a thorough discussion with PW 1. who lodged the purported first information report Exhibit 1 dated 4-11-1975, yet the same does not disclose any reference whatsoever about the telephonic conversation from Bangabhaban with them at the Central Jail but the report allegedly submitted by PW 3 one day after i.e. on 05-11-1975 and marked as Exhibit 6 contains a vivid picture about the telephonic conversations from Bangabhaban by the accused persons with PW 3 and others at the Central Jail, at the early hours of 3-11-1975, such position along with other circumstances disclosed during his cross-examination by PW 3, as a matter of fact makes it quite probable, the defence suggestion that Exhibit 6 has been fabricated subsequently, for the purpose of this case. Therefore, we find no reason to differ with the trial Court that PW 3 is not a reliable witness.

259. PW 4 is a Jail Guard who disclosed in his deposition that 5 armed personnel who had entered inside the Central Jail all of whom were with black uniforms, therefore, he is contradicting the depositions of PWs 2 and 3 with respect of the colour of uniforms of the assailants. From a plain reading of his deposition it is found that he did not disclose the name of any of the accused except Moslemuddin. This witness also admitted in his cross-examination that they would not have allowed the 5 assailants to enter inside the Jail unless the Inspector General of Prisons, Deputy Inspector General of Prisons had given permission for their entrance. His deposition does not disclose the complicity of any other accused except Moslemuddin.

260. PW 5 is a gate sentry of Central Jail at the relevant time also deposed about the 5 armed personnel who had forced their entry inside the Jail and had committed the murder of 4 national leaders. In his evidence he did not however disclose the complicity of any of the accused except Captain Moslemuddin.

261. PW 6 Jail Guard also deposed that at the time of occurrence 4 army personnel with khaki uniform had entered inside the Jail and had committed the murders. This witness also does not disclose the name of any of the accused persons.

262. PW 7 Deputy Jailor also deposed that he was informed by the Jail guard that 4 persons with khaki uniforms had entered inside the Jail along with Inspector General of Prisons and Deputy Inspector General of Prisons he also did not disclose the complicity of any of the accused except Moslemuddin. He also admitted that he had not seen the occurrence by himself.

263. PW 8 another Deputy Jailor also deposed that he was informed by a gate sentry that 5 army personnel along with Inspector General of Prisons and Deputy Inspector General of Prisons had entered into the Central Jail, some time thereafter he had heard sounds, of gun shots. This witness also does not disclose the complicity of any of the accused persons.

264. PW 9 Chief Jail Guard also did not dis- close the complicity of any of the accused person.

265. PW 10 this witness also did not disclose the complicity of any of the accused persons. This witness in his cross-examination admitted to the effect:

“ জাতীয় ৪ নেতাকে কাহারা হত্যা করিয়াছে কাহারা জেলখানায় প্রবেশ করেন তাহা আমি বলিতে পারিব না।”

266. Before we deal with the witness from the side of Bangabhaban we feel it proper to note certain circumstances as disclosed by other witnesses and of them deposition of PW 29 is the most vital one. He is Colonel Shafayet Jamil and Brigade Commander of 46 Brigade, Dhaka at the relevant time. From his depositions it appears that he was the second man in the coup headed by Brigadier Khaled Mosharaf who was the Chief of General Staff at the relevant time. This witness deposed that they had decided to withdraw the infantry company from Bangabhaban at 12-00 midnight on November 2,1975 and this would carry a message of coup to the inmates of the Bangabhaban and as per their plan at 12-00 midnight of November 2, 1975 they had withdrawn 2 infantry companies to the Head Quarter from Bangabhaban. This witness deposed further that with a view to disconnect the Chief of Staff Ziaur Rahman from Bangabhaban a team of army personnel headed by Captain Hafizullah, were sent, Captain Hafizullah snapped the telephone line so that Khandaker Mostaque Ahmed and the rival force (inside the Bangabhaban) could not make any contact. This witness deposed further to the effect that it is under his command Radio and Television were stopped and officer commanding of Signal company Major Musa took control of Central Telephone Exchange, coupled with this deposition of PW 21 may be referred to in this connection who is Commodore Golam Rabbani, he was ADC to the President at the Bangabhaban at the relevant time i.e November 2, 1975. From his depositions it appears that he used to reside inside Bangabhaban and that on November 2, 1975 at about 11-00 PM he had gone for sleep at the 1st floor of Bangabhaban. At about 2-00 AM of November 3,1975 a messeger from President Mostaque was sent to him who having gone to him awoke him from sleep and was informed that his presence was desired by the President. Therefore, it is evident that when President wanted his ADC to talk the President had no other alternative but to send a messenger to him. At the same time we have noticed from the cross- examination portion of this witness PW 21 that there was a telephone link with his bedroom through which President could talk to him over the telephone if necessary. When such was the position what prompted the President to call him through a messenger as indicated above, the answer is that the telephone was not in operation, therefore, the President had to send a messenger to call his ADC.

267. In this context with reference to the aforesaid position we may refer to the deposition of PW 46. He is Lieutenant Colonel (Retd) Anowar-uz-zaman who at the relevant time was a Major and was the Commander of Rverine Support Unit at Sadarghat on November 2,1975. This witness is also a nephew of slain leader Syed Nazrul Islam. During cross-examination this witness depicted a picture to the effect that on 2-11-75 Khaled Mosharaf proclaimed a coup and they had gone to Bangabhaban but they could not capture power but on 3- 11-75 Khandaker Mostaque had to relinquish his power. This witness further deposed that on 2-11-75 the situation in the city was such that it was not possible on his part to collect information from the Central Jail for the sake of personal security. From the deposition of aforesaid 3 witnesses, it is palpably clear that the inmates of Bangabhaban received the message of a coup by their rival party at 12-00 mid- night to 1-00 AM on 3-11-75 it also indicates that the telephone link of Bangabhaban was snapped at that time so that the President and the army officers residing at Bangabhaban could not have any telephonic contact. It is revealed further from the aforesaid deposition that the inmates of Bangabhaban having received a message of coup by their rival party was not in a position to move outside Bangabhaban after 1-00 AM on November 3, 1975 because the situation was such that their personal security was very much at stake and it was very much known to them by way of withdrawal of the tanks from Bangabhaban and by deployment of their counter-force by way of a coup headed by Khaled Mosharaf as evident from the deposition of PW 29 who deposed to the effect:

“২রা নভেম্বর/৭৫ এর রাত্র ১২.০০/১.০০ টার পর Troops withdrow  সহ পরবর্তী আমাদের কর্মকান্ড Troops deploy  সহ ক্যান্টনমেন্ট হইতে সমস্ত কিছু পরিচালনা করা হয়। আবার ৩ তারিখ সকাল ভোর থেকে Troops deployment  শুরু হয়।”

This part of deposition of PW 29 shows that the troops were deployed by the authority which led the coup on November 2, 1975 who are undoubtedly rival party to the inmates of Bangabhaban at that time.

268. From the position as disclosed above by the witnesses in their depositions before the Court, it appears to us that it is very much doubtful as to whether there was at all any telephone link in operation between the Bangabhaban and any other part of the city like Central Jail, Dhaka. It is also evident from the deposition of the witnesses that on the night following 2-11-75 from 12-00 midnight to 1-00 AM the inmates of Bangabhaban had received the message that their rival force had already been deployed within the vicinity of Bangabhaban and the tanks meant for guarding Bangabhaban had already been withdrawn by their rival force. Therefore, it was humanely impossible on the part of the inmates of the Bangabhaban to go out of the gate mainly because of their personal security.

269. Under the given circumstances, the telephonic conversations from Bangabhaban to Central Jail as disclosed by the witnesses is very much difficult to be believed. Moreover, we find no reason to dis-agree with the learned Sessions Judge who after thorough analysis of their depositions found the testimonies of PWs 11, 13, 16, 17, 18 and 34 as unworthy of credence in the first part of his impugned judgment although he has contradicted his own findings at the later part of the same judgment. It is also evident from the deposition of PW 17 that the President could himself call anyone from his personal phone and that the President had his Military Secretary who used to remain at the disposal of the President round the clock and PW 17 and others had no authority to move a step without the permission from the Military Secretary and the ADC of the President. This witness appears to have disclosed the name of the Military Secretary wrongly. This also indicates that had he been in any service at Bangabhaban at the relevant time there was no reason why he should not know the name of the Military Secretary to the President, moreover these witnesses i.e PWs 11, 13, 16, 17, 18 and 34 were specifically suggested that they were not in service of Bangabhaban at the relevant time, though the suggestions were denied by this witnesses. Admitting to the effect that they had put their signatures in the duty register maintained at Bangabhaban, it was also suggested from the side of the defence that the duty register does not bear their signatures evidencing that they were on duty at the relevant time yet the duty register was not produced before the Court despite specific suggestion made to the witnesses in this regard. Non production of the duty register of Bangabhaban showing the signatures of this witnesses namely, PWs 11, 13, 16, 17, 18 and 34 warrants an adverse presumption under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. These circumstances coupled with the deposition of the witnesses as referred to above lead us to believe that the testimonies of those witnesses namely, PWs 11, 13, 16, 17, 18 and 34 are not trustworthy. We do not, in this regard find any reason to discard the finding of the trial Court in respect of the testimonies of those witnesses as available in the 1st part of his impugned judgment.

270. Turning to the deposition of PW 21 Commodore Golam Rabbani, ADC to the President at the relevant time. We may refer to the disclosure made by him during his cross-examination to the effect:

“ ২রা নভেম্বর/৭৫ সনে বঙ্গভবনের উপরে জংগী বিমান উড়ে। তবে হেলিকপ্টার বাহিরে উড়ে। টেলিফোন ও টেলিভিশনের যোগাযোগ বিচ্ছিন্ন ছিল।”

In view of the deposition as quoted above, and his deposition to the effect that he had found Major Rashid and Farook who were busy with telephone calls is not believable. We have also noticed from the deposition of PW 21 that he had not implicated any of the accused persons either in conspiracy or abetment except having found Major Rashid and Farook were busy with telephone calls although he has disclosed that the Resalder Muslemuddin. Dafader Marfat Ali Shah and LD (Dafader) Abul Hashem Mridha and others used to remain as personal guard of the President and he had found those persons were very much restive and they had gone out of Bangabhaban and had returned back at 6-00 AM on 3-11-75.

271. From the deposition of the witnesses III this case it is found that the prosecution has made an attempt to link the accused persons with the murder of 4 national leaders by disclosing the factum of telephonic conversation from Bangabhaban to Central Jail as also by the factum that some wit- nesses had found the accused persons engaged in deliberations in connection with Jail killing while others have come out to depose that Captain Moslemuddin along with 4 others had gone out of Bangabhaban at around 2-00 AM on the fateful night and had returned back at 6-00 AM on the next morning, thereby it is evident that the prosecution had made an abortive attempt to prove certain circumstances showing the complicity of the accused persons in the crime.

272. We do not feel it necessary to deal with other formal witnesses who have been brought before the Court for meeting up technicalities but none of them disclosed any complicity of the accused persons in the occurrence.

273. In this case both sides have produced certain decisions in support of their respective cases and Mr ASM Mobin, the learned Assistant Attorney- General, appearing on behalf of the State, submits that for the purpose of abetment as contemplated under section 107 of the Penal Code the prosecution need not prove any overt act and in substantiating his submission the learned Assistant Attorney- General cited the case of Abdul Awal vs State reported in 1994 BLD (AD) 224. On perusal of the said decision we find that in a wife killing case the husband had been convicted under sections 302/109 of the Penal Code although he was found to have been a silent spectator to the cruel and gruesome murder of his wife by his companions who were acquitted for want of legal evidence. It was reasonable to hold that though he could not be convicted under section 302 of the Penal Code but could be found guilty for abetment under sections 302/109 of the Penal Code. The facts of that case is completely different from one before us, therefore, the same is not applicable.

274. The learned Assistant Attorney-General placed reliance in the case of Baby John reported in 53 Criminal Law Journal 1273 (para-3). On perusal of the cited decision it appears to us that directions were given by the accused person to the effect that there must be force applied for any obstacles placed in their way by the Police or Army. In the evidence of that case PWs 75, 43, and 78 who had spoken about such directions given by the first accused to his audience, there was sufficient material for drawing the inference that there was instigation on the part of the 1st accused to the members of the procession and to the leaders of the processions that they must resist any opposition that might be offered by the police or by the Army and to see that the procession had gone from the point where it was to start and reached Quilion. When there was a prohibitory order issued by the District Magistrate, Quilion it was reasonable to presume that the 1st accused would have realised that so long as law and order were maintained in the state the authority concerned would not permit the ban to be ignored and processions taken which were expressly prohibited by the District Magistrate. Therefore, it was found that there was instigation to violate the order of the District Magistrate and it was rightly found that there was abetment. The facts of this case is completely different from the one cited by the learned Assistant Attorney-General therefore not applicable.

275. The other case relied by the learned Assistant Attorney-General in the case of G Ananthachari vs Crown reported in 40 Criminal Law Journal page 302 relevant page 304 where it has been held that in a case of abetment the law does not require that instigation should be in a particular form or that it should be only in words and may not be by conduct; for instance a mere gesture indicating "beat" or a mere offering of money by an arrested person to the constable who arrests him may be regarded as instigation, in the one case to beat and in the other to take a bribe. So far the principle enunciated in that case is concerned, there is no dispute at all, but each case is to be decided by its own merit, therefore, in the facts and circumstances of the present case we do not find any manner of application of that particular case referred by the learned Assistant Attorney-General.

276. It may not be out of context to mention that two of the condemned prisoners have been convicted under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code although they were charged under sections 302/109 of the Penal Code, in a situation like this the learned Assistant Attorney-General submits that even in the absence of charge under section 34 of the Penal Code their conviction can be maintained under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code although they were charged under sections 302/109 of the Penal Code.

277. In substantiating such submission the learned AAG has placed reliance in the case of S Satyanarayan vs Emperor reported in 45 Criminal Law Journal 624 (630) referring to the provisions of sections 236 and 237 of the Code of Criminal Procedure a Division Bench of Patna High Court, relying on a decision of the Privy Council in the case of Begu vs Emperor, quoted the decision as under:

"The illustration makes the meaning of these words quite plain. A man may be convicted of an offence, although there has been no charge in respect of it, if the evidence is such as to establish a charge that might have been made."

So far the principle enunciated in that particular decision, there is no dispute at all but under the facts and circumstances of the case before us we are to see as to whether the prosecution had brought home the charges against the condemned prisoners before us, beyond reasonable doubt.

278. The learned Assistant Attorney-General has placed before us the case of Javbanti Lal Ravji vs Emperor reported in 48 Criminal Lae Journal 419 (422) in that particular case it has been held by a Division Bench of Sind Chief Court, where the accused are charged of abetment of an offence, they can be convicted of the substantive offence if the accused had not been prejudiced in their defence of the case based on a substantive charge.

279. In this connection it may be mentioned that any defect in respect of a charge, do not ipso facto invalidate the conviction, unless it is shown that the defence has seriously been prejudiced because of the framing of the charge as available in a particular case. The question of prejudice is the only requirement on which the validity of the charge is to be determined.

280. In the case before us we are not so much concerned with the defect in the charge and the defence has also made no submission to that effect either, therefore the question having not been raised at the Bar, needs no decision merely for academic interest.

281. Mr ASM Abdul Mobin, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, submits further in reply to the defence submission that discrepancies in respect of the depositions of the witnesses occurs even in the evidence of a truthful witness and in substantiating his submission the learned Assistant Attorney-General placed reliance in the case of Ataur Rahman vs State reported in 43 DLR 87. From a perusal of the aforesaid decision it transpires that in that particular case a Division Bench of this Court having found 6 eye-witnesses available in support of the prosecution case and in relying on the witness who had himself sustained injury in the occurrence, it was held that "some discrepancies occurred in the witnesses of the prosecution but such discrepancies in the matter of detail of the incident always occurs even in the evidence of truthful witnesses."

282. Discrepancies and contradictions as contemplated under section 145 of the Evidence Act are two different things. The question in this particular case before us is not the same as was involved in the decision cited by the learned Assistant Attorney- General, therefore, we do not think it applicable in this case.

283. Pointing out the material omissions and contradictions in the statements of the witnesses upon whom the prosecution relied on very much. Mr Abdullah-al Mamun the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants has placed reliance in the case of NurulIslam vs State, reported in 1994 BLD (AD) 69 = 43 DLR (AD) 6.

284. From a perusal of the aforesaid judgment it appears that the High Court Division maintained the conviction imposed upon the appellants by the Sessions Judge without considering the omissions and contradictions available in respect of the depositions of the eye-witnesses and the said judgment or affirmance having been challenged before the Appellate Division, the aforesaid decision has been pronounced and upon consideration of the discrepancies, omissions and contradictions available on the testimonies of the witnesses, particularly of the so-called eye-witnesses their Lordships of the Appellate Division found that the High Court Division had not considered the material discrepancies, contradictions and omissions of the eye-witnesses, therefore, set aside the order of conviction and sentence passed by the trial Court and affirmed by the High Court Division. So far the principle of law laid down in the aforesaid judgment there is no dispute whatsoever, but we have to see whether there are contradictions or material omissions available in the case.

285. Mr Mamun having pointed out before us that in the instant case the prosecution has miserably failed to prove the factum of overt act or omission so as to suggest a preconcert or common design to commit the offence involved in this case, submits that the conviction under sections 302/109 of the Penal Code is not sustainable.

286. In substantiating his submission Mr Mamun placed reliance in the case of Ali Ahmed Malaker vs Slate reported in 43 DLR 401 wherefrom it appears that a Division Bench while dealing with a case under sections 302/\09 of the Penal Code has held that it is now well settled that to sustain a charge of abetment of offence it is necessary that there must be some evidence of overt act or omission so as to suggest a pre-concert or common design to commit a particular offence. So long as the design rests in intention short of overt act directed to the commission of the offence it is not indictable in law.

287. In appreciating the principle of law enunciated by the aforesaid decision we have also come across some decisions which have laid down that in sustaining a conviction under section 109 of the Penal Code in certain circumstances no direct overt act is necessary and in that line we have already referred the decisions cited by the learned Assistant Attorney-General which also refer to the indirect and implied overt acts.

288. On this principle of law Mr Mamun, has also placed reliance in the case of Murad Ali vs State reported in 22 DLR (WP) 158. From a perusal of the said judgment it appears that it was held that, to sustain a charge of abetment, it is necessary that there must be some evidence of an overt act or omission necessary so as to suggest a pre-concert or common design to commit a particular offence so long as the design rests in intention short of overt act directed to the commission of the offence it is not indictable in law.

289. We find that the same principle has been enunciated in the decision reported in 43 DLR 401 as referred to above and we have already expressed our reply to that decision as above.

290. Mr Mamun has also pointed to the facts involved in this case to the effect that all witnesses in this case have been examined by the Investigating Officer long after 21 years or even more, therefore, in view of the inordinate delay in examining the witnesses, renders the testimonies of the witnesses doubtful.

291. In substantiating his submission the learned Advocate has placed reliance in the case of Stale vs Monu Meah reported in 6 BLC 402 wherefrom it transpires that the testimonies of the eye-witnesses were treated to be doubtful because of the delay in examining those witnesses by 2 to 4 months by the Investigating Officer.

<u>292. In this connection we have to note that each case is to be decided by its own merit. Under certain circumstances delay of a few days even, may render the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses doubtful yet in other cases delay of years together may not do so.</u>

<u>293. In the instant case we have already noticed that it is a gruesome murder it was not allowed to be proceeded with for long about 21 years because of the existence of a hostile atmosphere therefore, mere delay in examination of the witnesses will not cast any doubt in the testimonies of the witnesses of this case, as was available in that particular case. In another case similar point has also been raised by Mr Abdulla-al-Mamun, which is the case of Moinullah vs State reported in 40 DLR 443 wherefrom it also appears that a similar principle of law has been enunciated, therefore, our answer is the same as to the previous one.</u>

<u>294. Pointing out the position that the conviction in the instant case has been based on circumstantial evidence, so far as it relates to the sections 302/109 of the Penal Code against the appellants. Mr Abdur Razzak Khan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants, has placed reliance in the case of Osman Gani vs State reported in 54 DLR (AD) 34. From a perusal of the aforesaid decision it transpires that their Lordships in the highest Court of the country have laid down the principle as under:</u>

<u>"The principle of circumstantial evidence to prove the guilt of an accused is that all the circumstances must themselves be proved beyond all reasonable doubt and the chain of circumstances should be so that the innocence of the accused is incompatible with the circumstances, if there be any missing link the accused will escape through it, for in that case the prosecution case will not be proved up to the hilt."</u>

<u>Mr Khan has also referred to the case of State vs Arman Ali reported in 42 DLR (AD) 50 wherefrom it transpires that their Lordships of the Appellate Division having enunciated the principle that in a case based on circumstantial evidence before any hypothesis of guilt is drawn up on the circumstances the legal requirement is to prove the circumstances themselves like any other fact beyond reasonable doubt.</u>

295. With reference to the aforesaid two decisions it may not be out of context to mention that in the instant case apart from the 3 condemned prisoners other appellants have been convicted under sections 302/109 of the Penal Code and the trial Court having relied on those circumstances brought by the prosecution witnesses based its conviction upon them, the circumstances are:

(1) There was a conspiracy by the accused persons at Bangabhaban for doing away with the 4 national leaders then confined in the Central Jail, Dhaka. So far as this part of the case is concerned the trial Court has already ruled it out altogether and acquitted all the accused persons under section 120B of the Penal Code, yet no appeal is preferred against such acquittal.

(2) The other circumstance that had been adduced by some of the PWs was that they had found those accused persons engaged in deliberations amongst themselves sitting within Bangabhaban.

(3) For proving such abetment the witnesses deposed that some of the accused persons had conversations and directions from Bangabhaban with the Jail authority.

(4) Another circumstance was that three condemned prisoners like other army officers, were detected by some of the witnesses to have gone out of Bangabhaban at about 3-00 AM on 3-11-75 and that they had returned back to Bangabhaban at dawn i.e at 6-00 AM, on the same day.

(5) There were telephonic conversations between the inmates of Bangabhaban and the Jail authority of Central Jail at and around the time of occurrence in connection with the brutal killing of the 4 national leaders.

These are all the circumstances on which the convictions have been awarded upon those accused persons residing in the Bangabhaban for abetment of the offence of murder under sections 302/109 of the Penal Code.

<u>296. On a careful scrutiny of the aforesaid two decisions pronounced by the apex Court we find that circumstances even if found to have been proved, in that case too there is a missing link or, in other words, it can be safely said that the circumstances available in the instant case even if proved by the prosecution in that case too those cannot lead us to any irresistible conclusion that there was no other hypothesis possible except the guilt of the accused persons rather the missing link in the chain of circumstances that has been proved even according to the prosecution, allows the accused persons to escape through the same, therefore, we are not in a position to sustain the conviction under sections 302/109 awarded upon the other appellants residing in Bangabhaban as has been held by the trial Court. More particularly, when as a matter of fact each of those circumstances involved in this case could not be proved beyond reasonable doubt and more so when the chain of circumstances are such that those are not at all incompatible with the innocence of the accused persons as we have already found that there is a missing link in the chain of circumstances through which the accused persons may find escape. Such as it was humanly impossible for any of the inmates of Bangabhaban to go out of the same at 00- 00 hours or afterwards on 3-11-1975 because of promulgation of the coup-d'etat by Khaled Musharaf on the same night and the consequent withdrawal of Tank Regiment from Bangabhaban as also for deployment of rival forces led by the leader of the coup, within the vicinity of Bangabhaban, at 12-00 hours of November 3, 1975.</u>

297. Now it is for this Court to see whether those circumstances themselves have been proved by the prosecution beyond reasonable doubt.

<u>298. We have already noticed that the factum of telephonic talk between the Bangabhaban and the Central Jail could not be proved to the hilt by the prosecution. We have also noticed that the trial Court has itself evaluated and rightly discarded the testimonies of the witnesses who deposed relating to the deliberations amongst the accused persons inside Bangabhaban over the killing of the 4 leaders.</u>

299. We have also noticed that we do not find any reason to disagree with the finding as arrived at by the trial Court, therefore, in our opinion, the decisions cited by Mr Khan in this connection as aforesaid fits in on all fours to this particular case.

300. It may be pointed out here that the defence case as it transpires from the trend of cross-examination of the witnesses was that at about 12 mid- night to 1-00 AM on 3-11-75 Khaled Mosharaf proclaimed a coup-d'etat thereby he along with PW 29 Colonel Shafayet Jamil withdrew the Tank Regiment from the Bangabhaban at 12-00 to 1-00 AM on 3-11-75 and it was the 4 leaders of Awami League who were the legitimate successors to the government after killing of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman; therefore, Khaled Mosharaf and his partymen with a view to secure their peaceful tenure of office, had killed those 4 leaders inside the Central Jail and the innocent accused persons have been falsely implicated upon fabricating documents.

301. In this connection the deposition of PW 52 Syed Mahbub-al-Karim, Special Officer to slain leader Syed Nazrul Islam is quoted below:

“ মোশতাক সরকারের বিরুদ্ধে অভ্যুত্থান ঘটানোর পরে, জিয়াউর রহমানকে বন্দী করার পরে, খালেদ মোশাররফ গংরা অভ্যুত্থানের মাধ্যমে প্রাপ্ত ক্ষমতা নিরংকুশ ভাবে ধরিয়া রাখার জন্য সেই মুহুর্তে প্রাপ্ত ক্ষমতায় বৈধ দাবীদার জেলখানায় থাকা নজরুল ইসলাম সাহেবদের হত্যার ষড়যন্ত্র করা হয় বলিয়া আমার ধারণা।”

This piece of evidence lends support to the defence version of the case and in a position like this the case of Muslimuddin vs State reported in 38 DLR (AD) 311 may be referred to wherefrom we find that the principle laid down in that case is that the fundamental principle of a criminal trial is that the accused shall be presumed innocent and that he is not required to adduce evidence to prove his innocence, but the entire burden of proof of his guilt lies on the prosecution alone and till that time the presumption of innocence continues, whether the case is before the trial Court or at higher forums..........................................................................................In a criminal case it is the duty of the Court to review the entire evidence that has been produced by the prosecution and the defence, if after an examination of the whole evidence, the Court is of opinion that there is reasonable possibility that the defence put forward by the accused might be true, it is clear that such a view reacts on the whole prosecution case. In these circumstances the accused is entitled to benefit of doubt, not as a matter of grace but as of right, because the prosecution has not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

302. In this connection we may also refer to the case of Safdar Ali vs Crown reported in 5 DLR (FC) 64. The said decision also expressed its opinion ill the similar language as arrived at by the Appellate Division, as mentioned above.

303. Turning to the case of 3 condemned prisoners, we find that they are (1) Resalder Moslemuddin alias Muslemuddin (Retd) alias Hiron Khan alias Muslemuddin (absconding) (2) Dafader Marfat Ali Shah (absconding) and (3) LD (Dafader) Md Abul Hashem Mridha (absconding). From the prosecution witnesses cited from the Central Jail, Dhaka none of them mentioned their names i.e the aforesaid two persons. In Exhibit 1 which was said to be the first information report. lodged first in point of time on 4-11-1975 that information does not contain names of two condemned prisoners i.e Dafader Marfat Ali Saha and LD (Dafader) Md Abul Hashem Mridha. Moreover PW 1 the informant has asserted in his deposition to the effect that all the 5 assailants who had gone to the Jail Gate and subsequently committed murder of the 4 leaders put their signatures in the gate register before their entrance inside the Jail and this PW 1 himself in his deposition in chief disclosed that it was at his asking all the 5 assailants put their signatures in the gate register, if. that be so in that case the gate register could have been the most vital document to connect all 5 assailants in this case but unfortunately, for the prosecution that gate register was not produced before the Court, therefore, it is rightly submitted by Mr Hannan that it warrants an adverse presumption in the prosecution case under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act.

304. From the deposition of PW 21 Commodore Golam Rabbani we find that he testified that the said two condemned prisoners along with others were found engaged as personal guard to the President and some time they were also found in a restive mood with arms, This witness further testified that Moslemuddin along with others had gone out of Bangabhaban at dawn and they had returned back at 6-00 AM on 3-11-75, PW 11 said that he had seen these two condemned prisoners along with others inside Bangabhaban. Similarly, PW 13 and 17 testified that these two condemned prisoners had gone out of Bangabhaban by Jeep at 3-00 AM on 3- 11-75 except the aforesaid 3 witnesses none else has disclosed the complicity of these two condemned prisoners. We have already noticed that the gate register where all the 5 assailants put their signatures has not been produced before this Court. It is in the evidence that these two condemned prisoners along with others were the personal guard of the President who were not supposed to leave the President at a stage when all the inmates of Bangabhaban had got the message that a coup had been declared headed by Khaled Mosharaf and in the meantime Tank Regiment had already been withdrawn from Bangabhaban and, as a matter of fact. there were no guards except those who were inside Bangabhaban, for the President, as it was revealed from PW 29 Shafayet Jamil.

305. Under such circumstances we are not in a position to accept the prosecution case that they, at such a grave moment could leave Bangabhaban for whatever purpose. Therefore, we find that the complicity of Dafader Marfat Ali Shah and LD (Dafader) Abul Hashem Mridha in connection with the kilIing of 4 leaders could not be proved to the hilt by the prosecution.

306. So far as Resalder Moslernuddin alias Mus- lemuddin (Retd) alias Hiron Khan alias Muslemuddin is concerned we find his presence throughout the entire prosecution case. From the first information report as claimed by the prosecution Exhibit 1 which was lodged on 4-11-75 after the occurrence that piece of paper also testifies that he entered into the Central Jail on the fateful night. True, it is that the description of Muslemuddin as disclosed by the prosecution differs from place to place though it could not be proved to the hilt by the prosecution that Muslemuddin came out of Bangabhaban and entered into the Central Jail yet it has been proved that he entered into the Central Jail on the fateful night irrespective of the place he came from, beyond reasonable doubt, therefore, Muslemuddin cannot absolve his liability in this case.

307. There is no denial of the fact that the occurrence that had taken place inside the Central Jail, Dhaka was not only gruesome murder but also alrocious and cowardly too, since the 4 national leaders were done to death during their captivity.

<u>308. True, it is that it was the failure on the part of the Investigating Officer to detect all the 5 assailants who had entered inside the Jail, otherwise none of them could deserve any sort of lenient attitude from the Court because of their involvement in such a horrendous crime, but these 2 condemned prisoners namely Dafader Marfat Ali Shah and LD Dafader Abul Hashem Mridha cannot be connected with the crime beyond reasonable doubt, therefore, we are of the considered opinion that this two condemned prisoners are entitled to be acquitted on the principle of benefit of doubt.</u>

309. So far as the other 4 appellants before us namely, Lieutenant Syed Farook Rahman, Lieutenant Colonel Sultan Shahriar Rashid Khan, Major (Retd) BazlulHuda and Major AKM Mohiuddin Ahmed are concerned we have already found that their complicity in the instant case could not also be proved by the prosecution to the hilt. Therefore, these 4 appellants are also entitled to get the benefit of doubt.

310. In view of what has been stated above, the Death Reference is hereby accepted in part so far as it relates to Resalder Moslemuddin alias Muslemuddin (Retd) alias Biron Khan alias Muslemuddin. But the same so far as it relates to Dafader Marfat Ali Shah (absconding) and LD (Dafader) Md Abul Hashem Mridha, is rejected and accordingly, they are entitled to be acquitted of the charges leveled against them.

The appeals brought by the 4 appellants namely, Lieutenant Syed Farook Rahman, Lieutenant Colonel Sultan Shahriar Rashid Khan, Major (Retd) Bazlul Huda and Major AKM Mohiuddin Ahmed are also allowed and the order of conviction and sentence passed against them by the Metropolitan Sessions Judge in Sessions Case No. 7 of 1999 are hereby set aside. They are acquitted from the charges leveled against each of them and they be set at liberty forthwith, if not wanted in this connection with any other case.
